And My Life... [finally I did put it into words!]

September 25, 2005

Itchy, titchy, but bitchy all the same — that’s how life is. I’m not here to boast about how tough things have been, or to fish for anyone’s sympathy; if anything, even I’m not entirely sure why I’m making this so-called public confession.

I’ve always wondered how and when people start feeling the need to document their lives. The bigger question is why at all. Aren’t we content leaving our lives as a black box, letting no one see the underside of that decaying smile? I’ve never been able to answer that, even for myself. I’ve never been one for talking things through — I’m a loner, someone who’s worked everything out alone. Whatever I’ve made of my life, good or bad, comes down to my own choices and instincts. If nothing else, you can’t blame me for it.

This is going to be a long story — it doesn’t have names in it, only people, people who mean far more to me than names ever could. If you’re reading this, it’s because I’ve found the courage to trust you with it. Some of it might leave you a little wide-eyed. My life hasn’t always been pretty, and the smile I wear day to day has very little to do with what’s underneath it.

It starts like any family story: parents, two kids. I was the youngest — meant to be the spoiled one, meant to grow up burning through my father’s savings on whims the way most of my cousins did. That never happened. Instead my life turned into a skid mark with the burning smell of rubber behind it. I hate that smell — it doesn’t just make me sick, it seems to kill off good brain cells too, or so my own overthinking mind decided after years of brooding on it. I never felt smarter for breathing in that choking, worthless smoke; if anything, I felt duller for it. Maybe that proves the point.

Now rewind thirteen years — I’ve lost the exact count by now. You’d see a family of four blooming in a small countryside town. We had it all: love, peace, every smile we needed.
I was around eleven, not old, but I’d already seen enough. I watched my dad’s grin the day he became an important political figure, playing by his own rules and principles. I won’t pretend to know just how honest a man he was — only that he was good enough for ordinary people to back him, and good enough to make his corrupt opposition hate him for it. He’d seen life, and so had the rest of us alongside him. I remember when he was framed for a murder he never committed — politics can turn ugly fast when you refuse to let politics stay politics. He told me later about the cold nights he spent hiding in the sugarcane and paddy fields with nothing to cover himself, while his closest friends worked to prove his innocence. The humiliation ended when the real culprit was caught and tried. My mother cried herself to sleep most nights, and sometimes just cried, full stop. I was too busy building castles out of G.I. Joe figures and Hot Wheels — to me it was just another year of school.
Not long after, the Hindu-Muslim riots broke out and the whole town turned hungry for blood. Every man in the house was posted on the terrace, firing into the air — a hooligan’s festival no one actually enjoyed. My father stood watch on our terrace with a rifle to scare off anyone trying to break in, while the rest of us slipped through connecting neighborhood windows into the hidden basement of a temple our family owned. My lips were dry, my throat choked with tears, and I don’t remember much else from that night except how certain I was that none of us would make it. All the women and children locked themselves in the largest room of the temple and got through that night of gunfire on nothing but the sound of each other’s breathing. In those moments, my father and his rifle were the only thing that felt like hope — hope built on the fact that the same rifle could just as easily take hope from someone else’s life. Life has a way of being ironic like that.

And this is only the beginning. I haven’t even started. Keep in mind — through all this, a family of four was still, somehow, blooming toward something good. And it was.

I had never seen my mother cry that hard. All I knew was that on an unexpected day off from school, something must have gone badly wrong. I still remember her hugging me in despair, holding on so tightly it felt like she was trying to pass part of her own life into me while praying for someone else’s. My father had been in a serious accident — thought dead, left by the roadside under a sheet. Hours passed before, by coincidence, one of my uncles happened to drive by. He was a doctor, and shocked to find him there. It was clear the odds were grim — the injury was to the head, the blood loss immense. To make things worse, the nearest hospital equipped to handle it was nearly 300 kilometers away. I don’t know who drove that day. I just thank him, whoever he was, with everything I have.
While everyone rushed off with what looked like a body already gone, I was left standing at a fork in the road — one way led to the hospital, the way my father had already gone; the other led home, which was just a house without him now.

Two months in a coma inside the ICU — that was my father’s. Two months in a coma outside it — that was my mother’s. She never left his side, not even in his most abandoned hour. The life support machine kept him breathing, alongside her unbroken prayers. He lived to tell the story. He lived because he’d never smoked, because he’d never touched liquor, and because all of us needed him too badly for him not to. But he lived only after a brain hemorrhage, paralysis down his right side, and total memory loss.
For a while, my mother and sister were just nurses to him, doctors were doctors, and friends were strangers. Me? I was still his son. That was the one thing he remembered. I was eleven, and even then I understood something about how powerful real love is — how it can override logic and the certainty of medicine. That one surviving memory of me was the best gift a father could give his son.

He couldn’t speak. He saw four of everything. He couldn’t walk, couldn’t help with anything practical while my mother carried the weight of his daily care alone. But I remember his eyes — full of questions, frowning at every unfamiliar face around him, and then lighting up in the widest smile the moment I came near.

I was there the day he beat his own feeding system by drinking a glass of milk on his own, just because I’d asked him to. The doctors were stunned. That was the day I started to understand the sheer will behind that unreadable face.

He recovered, against everything the doctors predicted. But the heavy antibiotics left their mark — his emotions came out now as sudden anger or tears he couldn’t hold back. A man who never shed a single tear through all of it now cries within seconds of hearing my voice on the phone. He also gained weight he can’t stand and can’t exercise away. Life has its own sense of humor.
My mother has always been the quiet one through all of it — endless patience, endless endurance, more than I ever inherited from her. Her faith has never once wavered, and somehow I know it never will. She’s a woman built entirely of belief.

The whole family got through this leaning on a business that was slowly declining even as it kept us afloat. My father went through a few smaller accidents after that too — a broken arm that needed steel rods, a leg he nearly lost to infection, other injuries that only look minor in hindsight.

Alongside all this, other parts of life kept moving. My sister found the man she wanted to spend her life with, and no matter how much my parents disapproved, she was determined to be heard and to marry him anyway. I was the only one on her side — simply because I liked him. My mistake, as it turned out.

It’s strange how a small town with such a predictable life still finds endless things to gossip about — and it’s not remotely funny how quickly relatives start reaching for money that was never theirs, regardless of who it actually belongs to. My family wasn’t blessed with the best relatives in that respect. In the movies, no one gets to seize the land and hard-earned property of a man who knows how to fight for himself but is now too weak to fight back. In real life, they absolutely can.

All the talk of brotherly love and concern turned out to be hollow — just words with nothing behind them. Greed took over completely, and it’s unsettling how ugly greed can make people. Threats, attempted assaults, and things of that nature became disturbingly routine.

A few years before all this, I’d already moved to another city to build a career, because my mother — always the one looking ahead — couldn’t see a future for me surrounded by people who valued the smell of money over anything else. I should have realized sooner that it’s the smell of minted coins, not printed books, that runs this world.

No one in my family told me any of this directly. I only learned about it later, through cousins who liked eavesdropping on their parents’ conversations. I lived through those moments of helplessness carrying a quiet “I will make them pay one day” feeling. Somewhere in me, that instinct is still lurking.

My sister eventually got the wedding she deserved, full of love, to the man she’d dreamed about. But even through all of it, I could see something on my mother’s face — beneath the sense of duty, a quiet disappointment she never voiced. And if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s this: never question a mother’s instincts.

By then my family had split into fronts. I was fighting to build my own way up. My sister was learning to live under the weight of new responsibilities. My parents were fighting off a pack of relatives circling everything my father had built in his prime — soon joined, unsurprisingly, by their own son-in-law, who turned out to be a genuinely awful person.

I was coping, but the pressure showed by the end of most days. Those years in school hostel taught me a new way to live — a kind of split personality, and it’s stuck with me since. One half kept every private, decaying log of life buried in pages and in the heart. The other was the easygoing wrapper the rest of the world got to see. Those last two years of school made me as hard to read as I ever wanted to be. Of every face I saw, there was only one I actually fell for. No, I wasn’t the type to act on it back then — maybe I would be now, but not then. I finished school without ever saying anything meaningful to her, telling myself it was just infatuation, and let her pass by like a fragrance that didn’t really matter.

I’d once dreamed of being a world-renowned businessman. I gave that up for the safer path of engineering, and it worked out well enough — I took to computers and found real contentment in it. I’ve always leaned optimistic, and things do tend to turn out fine eventually. My parents became grandparents when I became an uncle, and it finally felt like we were headed toward better days — a feeling we hadn’t had in years. He was the thread that was going to hold all of us together.
Around then I ran into the girl I’d never spoken to in school, this time online. She became my closest friend — still is. What you couldn’t get out of me in years, she could get in five minutes flat, just by talking to me. Things were looking up. But dreams, as they say, have a habit of turning the moment you stop watching them.

My sister’s marriage started falling apart. Her husband shut down the small business my parents had set up for him, hoping instead to get his hands on my father’s. His own family had already lost everything of theirs for reasons no one fully explained. My sister decided to leave. He wouldn’t let her go easily — doing so would have cost him his last shot at everything he’d been counting on.

Living alone with a child, while still technically married, and holding onto your dignity without leaning on anyone — not even your own brother — isn’t an easy way to live. The pressure catches up eventually. You become a vessel trying to hold more than it’s built for, and every so often it spills over the edges. It’s a hard life. And the hardest part of all is the question a small child eventually asks about a parent who isn’t there.

Letting go of the people closest to you is never simple. After three years of turning the same thoughts over, I finally understood that what I felt for someone was closer to infatuation than love, and that realization became more of a quiet reckoning than a decision. But nothing lasts forever — the oldest rule there is.
She left for reasons that stayed unclear, at least to me. I was back at square one, wondering what I could have done differently. Probably nothing. If there had been something, I’d have already done it.

I’d already found a stable job by then and put everything I had into it, believing that enough hard work and honesty would eventually pay off. But I never did inherit my mother’s kind of persistence.

It’s strange how hollow and broken people can become without it ever showing on the surface — how someone can end something as precious as a life just because the one path they were counting on for a comfortable future closed on them. My brother-in-law killed himself. It left me with pity for his parents, a complicated, quiet relief for my sister, deep grief and worry for my nephew, and a kind of numbness toward the man himself. I won’t speak ill of someone who’s gone, but he’d done more than enough, while he was here, to earn the anger I still carry for him.

Along the way I’ve met other people who’ve mattered. I’ve changed a lot — from someone introverted, unsure, and apprehensive into someone who doesn’t second-guess himself, who knows what he wants. Life has its own cruel, effective way of teaching its hardest lessons. There’s one year in particular that was probably the most dramatic stretch of all this, and even now I’d rather skip past it. Some things just aren’t meant to be said out loud.

More happened in the middle of all this — things worth mentioning, and yet too private to put into words. Somewhere in me, that closed-off part of myself is still there, still working through it.

My family: a man who never gave up on life. A woman who made a few hasty, wrong decisions but can’t fairly be blamed for them — she holds a kind of respect no one else in my life ever will. A young mother with the courage to stand against the world for what she believes, who will keep fighting for the acceptance and respect she deserves. I don’t know which of these traits I carry. All I know is that I have hope. You know what they say about hope:
“Hope is one of the good things, maybe the best of things, and good things never die.” — The Shawshank Redemption

I’ve written this for a few reasons. First — as my friend, you’ve earned the right to see into my life, but I’d ask that it stays between us. Know that I’ve shared this only after a great deal of thought and hesitation. Second, this isn’t self-pity — I wanted a record of the hardest days, so that someday, looking back, I can say: you’ve come a long way, and someone up there must be looking out for you. And third, to mark this as the day I decided to stand up, however hard it takes, for my parents against anyone who thinks it’s easy to come after my family and walk away clean.

I’m the son my parents had after losing their first child, four months after he was born. I’ll spend my life trying to live up to whatever they might have hoped for him, had he stayed. I know my mother still misses him quietly, even if she’s never said so.

It runs in my family — we don’t give up. If you ever want to understand us, look at the eyes: my father’s, always carrying helplessness and love in equal measure. My mother’s, full of unshakeable faith and the will to keep standing for her children, for her family, for anything that matters to her. My sister’s, holding onto hope — for herself, and for everything good she wants for her son. And mine — always searching, trying to find whether there’s a divided self hiding in you too.
This is my life, for anyone who’s ever wondered what’s behind that easy laugh. I hope that answers it.

Well, below this you’ll find a lot of things written over the years. The timestamps are all new, since I moved this over to a different blog a while back — these are just a few pieces pulled from the recent past. Most of the rest is still buried somewhere in this endless pile of old words.
